differences.how: the build has no stack there. Through the engraving's camera this stack, carried up past the remodel's mansard to about 15.9 m, stands at x 672 px with its top at y 113, which is where the engraving draws the stack the build reads as the wing's (x 663-717, top y 113; T-2465 put it at u 10.2, v 11.2, top 15.11 m). Through this camera the build's wing stack falls at x about 75 px, where the photograph shows sky between the branches, but this photograph predates the wing. So the engraving's stack is either this one carried up or a new one on the wing: T-2756 weighs the two and builds the one the evidence holds

differences.what: the cornice: a deep dark band round the eave on the front and the south flank, its top against the sky on the build's slope through this camera (0.19 on the flank, 0.21 on the front)

Its brackets are too dark here to count, and this photograph cannot measure the eave's height (the camera's solve: the band's height sets it, and the fence hides the ground), so the engraving's storey-line item, open in its own record, stays the place the eave's height is argued

evidence_of_its_own_date: The photograph is the Grosvenor house as built, c. 1870, before Jesse Spalding's remodel; the 1904 scene is the remodelled house, which the engraving draws from the north-west and the 1911 Sanborn sheet plans. So each thing this photograph shows is weighed (AGENTS.md rule 11, T-2449): where the engraving or the sheet shows the remodel KEPT it, it is built and reads fixed, or is open until it is (T-2756); where they show the remodel REPLACED it, it is argued not shown for 1904 with the later evidence named. Where neither later witness can see it (the south flank, which the engraving faces away from), the masonry is read as kept: a remodel that recast the front and the roof is not evidence that it took down a side wall's bay, and the 1911 sheet still draws one there.
